Zcash developers urge users to move ~$300M out of the legacy Sapling pool –
Link
Zcash developer Zakura is calling for an end to new deposits into the legacy Sapling pool, which still holds about 400,000 ZEC (~$300M). The team warns that future math breakthroughs could let attackers forge Sapling proofs, and recommends moving funds to Ironwood, which already holds ~85% of shielded ZEC. Withdrawals would stay open, and no activation date has been set.
Retiring legacy cryptography before it breaks is a proactive security move, and it strengthens Zcash's long-term case as a privacy chain.

tweet.text:
As I mentioned in my previous tweet, the new US restrictions on remote access to advanced compute could have very different implications across the forward curve.

In the short term, restrictions on Chinese customers accessing GPUs overseas could release existing capacity back into the rental market, putting downward pressure on spot prices.

In the medium to long term, however, regulatory uncertainty, a shrinking addressable customer base, and heightened underwriting risks could discourage financing and new GPU deployments in Asia. Nvidia’s reported shipment halt further reinforces this supply-side risk.

The paradox: the same regulatory intervention could increase available supply today while reducing incremental supply tomorrow.

The implications for GPU rental prices are therefore highly duration- and geography-dependent. Near-term bearishness does not necessarily translate into lower forward prices.

Watch the forward curve, not just the spot price.

1Password reports security breach
Password manager 1Password has disclosed a security incident that occurred on November 19. Users were notified about it by email.
According to the company, attackers gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account and stole 1Password source code. They also managed to access company systems and obtain some customer information, including:
• Names and email addresses
• Account identifiers
• Public cryptographic keys
• Tokens from some account recovery links
1Password says users' vault contents, including passwords, secrets and other stored items, as well as the keys protecting them, were not compromised.
The company warns users to watch out for potential phishing attempts. No changes to 1Password accounts are required.

Ethereum L2s paid mainnet just $630K this year, down 99% from 2023 –
Link
Ethereum Layer 2s have paid only about $630K in fees to mainnet since the start of 2026, compared with $150M in 2023. Over the same period, L2 transaction volume grew from 900M to 7.4B. Blobs have pushed rollup data costs close to zero, so Ethereum now earns roughly 8 cents for every 1,000 L2 transactions.
L2 scaling is working for users, but it has not turned into fee revenue for ETH. That keeps the debate over L1 value accrual and ETH's economic model alive.

tweet.text:
Ethereum layer 2s have paid Ethereum just $0.63M in rent in 2026 so far, down from $150M in 2023, even as their transactions rose from 0.9 billion to 7.4 billion a year.

Blobs made rollups almost free to run, but Ethereum now earns about 8 cents per 1,000 layer 2 transactions, which weakens the idea that layer 2 growth feeds ETH value.

CZ Urges 1Password Users to Change All Passwords After Security Breach

1Password, a leading password management provider, disclosed a security breach in which attackers compromised an employee's corporate GitHub account, injected malicious code into backend systems and stole customer information, including names, email addresses, account identifiers and certain invitation and recovery tokens.

Attackers also accessed private source code and the company's CI/CD system. 1Password said customer vaults, passwords and encryption keys remained secure, with no evidence of account takeovers. Binance founder CZ nevertheless urged users to change all their passwords, calling it "a pain in the neck, but necessary."
